<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="1">Introduction</head><p>Recent advances in Large Language Model (LLM) based agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Park et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Yao et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Richards and et al., 2023)</ref> have demonstrated remarkable success across various tasks, including code generation <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Wu et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Guo et al., 2024)</ref>, mathematical reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Swan et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Yu et al., 2024)</ref>, and embodied actions <ref type="bibr">(Wang et al.</ref>, 2023). Building on the impressive capabilities of single agents, the LLM-based Multi-Agent System (MAS) has been proposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Park et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Du et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr">Hong et al., 2023)</ref> to harness the collective intelligence and specialized expertise of multiple agents. As the pool of available LLMs continues to grow <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chang et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Minaee et al., 2024)</ref>, how to select the appropriate LLM to power single agents or MAS has increasingly captured the attention of the research community <ref type="bibr">(Hu et al., 2024a;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b1">akota et al., 2024)</ref>. One might assume that, disregarding cost, choosing the largest LLM would always yield the best performance. However, larger LLMs have been shown to not always outperform their smaller counterparts <ref type="bibr">(Abdin et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Lepagnol et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Shen et al., 2024)</ref>. At times, smaller LLMs can achieve superior performance at a lower computational cost. Given this context, how to dynamically route the most appropriate LLM to empower an agent in a query-aware manner emerges as a highly compelling problem.</p><p>To address this, LLM routing is proposed to intelligently assign the optimal LLM for each query <ref type="bibr">(Hu et al., 2024a;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Srivatsa et al., 2024)</ref>. Early attempts employ a router, typically based on encoder models like BERT <ref type="bibr">(Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>, to make a binary decision on whether to select a larger LLM <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2023a;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Ding et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Ong et al., 2024)</ref>. More recent practices construct a router to assess the performance and cost of multiple LLMs, subsequently selecting the model that optimizes the trade-off between exploration and exploitation <ref type="bibr">(Dai et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Mohammadshahi et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Feng et al., 2024)</ref>. Although existing LLM routing methods <ref type="bibr">(Hu et al., 2024a;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Stripelis et al., 2024)</ref> have been proven effective in directing the most appropriate LLM for input queries, they are limited to single-agent scenarios <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Wei et al., 2022;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Shinn et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Reworkd, 2023)</ref> yet not ready for MAS. However, we argue that the availability of a routing method for MAS is even more essential. On the performance perspective, multi-agent systems have been proven to outperform single-agent approaches significantly <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2023b;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Pina et al., 2023)</ref>. On the cost perspective, though impressive in performance, existing multi-agent pipelines inherently introduce substantial token overhead and increased economic costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Zhuge et al., 2024)</ref>, which further necessitates the use of routing to mitigate overhead. In this context, there is a critical need to address this gap: How can we effectively route LLMs for MAS to balance performance and costs?</p><p>A seemingly intuitive solution is to directly transfer single-agent LLM routing methods to MAS. However, MAS needs to select the appropriate agent collaboration modes <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Du et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2024c)</ref> for different tasks and establish a reasonable division of labor <ref type="bibr">(Hong et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>, which previous routing methods fail to achieve. For example, for software development tasks, an ideal MAS routing method could design a hierarchical workflow with sequential steps such as requirements analysis, algorithm design, code development, and testing, each requiring corresponding role profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ramin et al., 2020;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Zingg et al., 2023)</ref>. Against this backdrop, we argue that routing in MAS involves more tasks than just LLM recommendations: ❶ Collaboration Mode Determination: Choosing the optimal communication mechanisms (e.g., Chain <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Qian et al., 2023)</ref>, Tree <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Ishibashi and Nishimura, 2024)</ref>, Graph <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hao et al., 2023)</ref>) for varying task complexities. This involves identifying the most efficient and adaptable multi-agent topology <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Zhuge et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2024a</ref>) that minimizes overhead while ensuring flexibility and scalability in more complex scenarios. ❷ Dynamic Agent Number: Determining the number of expert agents required <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Huang et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Aghdam et al., 2024)</ref> based on the difficulty of the input. ❸ Agent Role Allocation: Selecting suitable role to the agent according to the query domain <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2023b;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Feng et al., 2024)</ref> to ensure efficient task division, creating a system greater than the sum of its parts <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Shang et al., 2024)</ref>. ❹Agent LLM Routing: Assigning each agent the appropriate LLM based on the collaborative topology and the role of each LLM <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Feng et al., 2024)</ref>.</p><p>In light of the scrutinizing challenges, we for the first time introduce the concept of LLM-based ::</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head>Multi-::</head><p>Agent : System :: Routing (MASR): Multi-Agent Systems Routing (MASR): Given a pool of available LLMs, collaborative communication modes, and possible agent roles, an optimal MAS Router for any query q should: (1) identify appropriate multi-agent collaboration modes, (2) allocate agent roles efficiently, and (3) assign the appropriate LLM to each agent, thereby balancing performance and cost.</p><p>The formal definition of MASR is provided in Section 3. To construct a router that ideally adheres to the MASR principles, we propose an effective, token-economical, and inductive LLM-powered ::</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head>Multi-:</head><p>Agent : System :::::: Router, termed MasRouter. Technically, MasRouter integrates collaboration mode determiner, agent role allocator, and agent LLM router into a unified routing framework: ❶ Collaboration determiner employs a variational latent variable model to route the user query to a suitable collaboration module; ❷ Role allocator progressively generates agent roles through a structured probabilistic cascade; ❸ LLM router models the LLM backbone recommendation for each agent as a multinomial distribution problem. Ultimately, MasRouter constructs a MAS that simultaneously balances effectiveness and efficiency.</p><p>Our contributions can be summarized as follows:</p><p>• Problem Definition.</p><p>We for the first time formally define Multi-Agent System Routing (MASR), which specifies the requirements for MAS routing: assigning the appropriate collaboration mode, agent roles, and LLMs to each query, thereby improving response quality and reducing unnecessary overhead. • Practical Solution. We propose MasRouter, a modular MASR solution that utilizes a cascaded controller network to construct a highperforming and resource-efficient MAS progressively. Besides, MasRouter can seamlessly integrate with mainstream MAS to achieve efficient routing with significantly lower inference cost. • Experimental Validation. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks show that MasRouter is: (I) high-performing, surpassing RouterDC, the state-of-the-art routing method, by 3.51% on average; (II) economical, reducing the overhead on HumanEval from 0.363$ to 0.185$; (III) inductive and plug-and-play, generalizing to unseen LLM backbones and collaboration modes and seamlessly combining with mainstream multiagent systems with 17% ∼ 28% ↓ fewer cost.</p><p>2 Related Work Multi-Agent System. Contemporary LLMbased multi-agent systems (MAS) can be broadly categorized into two paradigms: (1) Fixed agentic networks with pre-established, manually crafted architectures, from debate <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chan et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Liang et al., 2023)</ref>, collaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Yin et al., 2023;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Wang et al., 2024)</ref> to competetive <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Zhao et al., 2023)</ref>. MacNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Qian et al., 2024)</ref> systematically analyzed typical multi-agent collaboration topologies such as chain, tree, graph, etc.; (2) Dynamic agentic networks that configure their structure and communication strategies based on real-time feedback and observations. ADAS <ref type="bibr">(Hu et al., 2024b)</ref> and its follow-up works <ref type="bibr">(Zhang et al., 2024c;</ref><ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Shang et al., 2024)</ref> leverage search methods such as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and evolutionary algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Zhang et al., 2025)</ref> to discover effective agent strategies. Other works like DyLAN <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Liu et al., 2023)</ref>, GPTSwarm <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Zhuge et al., 2024)</ref> and AgentPrune <ref type="bibr">(Zhang et al., 2024a)</ref> dynamically optimize the inter-agent topologies. Nevertheless, contemporary MAS is often LLM-homogeneous, i.e., relying exclusively on the same LLM backbone, failing to collectively organize heterogenous LLM-agents.</p><p>Single LLM Routing Efficient routing strategies for single LLMs have been extensively explored to balance computational cost and model performance. Early attempts on LLM routing include HybridLLM <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ding et al., 2024)</ref>, RouteLLM <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Ong et al., 2024)</ref> and FrugalGPT <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2023a)</ref>, which primarily focus on binary routing and leverage techniques like sequential pipelines or preference-driven routing to enhance decisionmaking performance. More recent practices, including Rootoo <ref type="bibr">(Dai et al., 2024)</ref>, C2MAB-V (Mohammadshahi et al., 2024), GraphRouter <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Feng et al., 2024)</ref> and RouterDC <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Chen et al., 2024)</ref> have shifted towards multi-choice selection frameworks. However, existing routing methodologies mainly focus on single-agent scenarios, and their unawareness of inter-agent topology constrains their applicability to more complex tasks and limits scalability in larger systems.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="3">Formalization</head><p>In this section, we formalize our proposed LLMbased Multi-Agent System Routing (MASR) and introduce its optimization objectives.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="3.1">Notation Establishment</head><p>Search Space. We first define the search space of a multi-agent system as S = (M, R, T), where M denotes the pool of N m available LLM backbones, R represents the set of N r predefined agent roles (e.g., analyst, programmer, and tester), and T denotes the set of N t collaboration modes, including structures like Chain, Tree, LLM-Debate, etc. Within the search space, a multi-agent system instance is defined as follows:</p><p>Definition 1 (Multi-Agent System) The MAS S combines several specific LLM-powered agents with distinct identities, working together collaboratively:</p><formula xml:id="formula_0">S = {{M i } k i=1 , {R i } k i=1 , T }, M i ∈ M, R i ∈ R, T ∈ T,<label>(1)</label></formula><p>where M corresponds to the selected LLM backbones and, similarly, R and T represent the chosen role and collaboration mode respectively. k denotes the number of the LLM agents.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="3.2">Definition of MASR</head><p>Based on the MAS defined above, we formalize Multi-Agent Systems Routing (MASR):</p><p>Definition 2 (MASR) MASR can be represented by the mapping function f , which maps from S = (M, R, T) to a MAS S tailored for the query Q:</p><formula xml:id="formula_1">f : M × R × T - → S, π (S) = P {M i } k i=1 , {R i } k i=1 , T | Q , M i ∈ M, R i ∈ R, T ∈ T, S ⊂ S (2)</formula><p>where π (S) represents the probability of selecting multi-agent system S, conditioned on Q.</p><p>Optimization Objective. Given a benchmark D consisting of multiple queries Q and corresponding oracle answers a, the ideal MASR aims to optimize</p><p>Collaboration Modes Agent Routing Optimize Query-specific Collab representation SC Ensemble Macnet(Chain) Star LLM Debate Module Encoder Collaboration Assignment Sentence Bert; MiniLM; ... As a physicist, I would apply the physical principles to analyze the query. The key physical formula is: and As a test engineer, I will verify if the programmer's code conforms to the problem logic and give the checked code: [Python Code] Collaborative reasoning Workflow Solution to task Based on the discussions, the answer is a speed of approximately 1.53 m/s at which the motor can lift 6 kg mass. ▶ Input query ▶ Collaboration Determination ▶ Agent Role Allocation ▶ Agent LLM Routing ▶ Collaborative Reasoning Materials 🤔 Query/Problem An electric motor has a label on it that reads: Input: 120V AC, 1.0 Amps, 60 Hz -Efficiency -75%. At what constant speed can the motor lift up a 6 kg mass? 🤖 LLM set 🧰 Collaboration Repo 🎭 Role pool Programmer Math Analyst Physicist ... Test Engineer Macnet(Chain) Self-Consistency Ensemble ... ... (Other Collaboration Modes) LLM Debate Macnet(Star) Difficulty Measure Agent Count Mode Prob. Distribution 1 2 3 4 5 6 Collaboration Determiner: SC is not sufficiently effective Debate incurs excessive costs Chain has achieved a balance Agent Role & LLM Routing Role Router: LLM Router : Programmer Math Analyst Test Engineer Physicist As a mathematician, I will follow the physicist's analysis and perform calculations step by step: ... As a programmer, I will list the code according to the mathematician's formula to prevent calculation errors: [Python Code]</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head>Output solution</head><p>The agent needs a role to conduct an overall analysis of this physics problem a strategy to jointly balance performance and cost.</p><p>The objective function is defined as:</p><formula xml:id="formula_2">max P(S|Q) E (Q,a)∼D, S∈S∼P(S|Q) U (S; Q, a) U tility -λ • C(S; Q) Cost , (<label>3</label></formula><formula xml:id="formula_3">)</formula><p>where P(S|Q) represents the probability distribution of S conditioned on Q. The utility term U (S; q, a) measures the performance of the MAS, while the cost term C(S; q) quantifies the expected cost (e.g., LLM calls, API cost, token cost). λ is a trade-off parameter.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="4">MasRouter</head><p>Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> illustrates the overall framework of MasRouter. For a given query, MasRouter samples the customized components of the MAS, through the collaboration determiner (▷ Section 4.1), role allocator (▷ Section 4.2), and agent LLM router (▷ Section 4.3), together forming a task-adaptive MAS S. After executing the sampled MAS, MasRouter jointly optimizes the parameters of each selection module based on the performance/cost feedback (▷ Section 4.4).</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="4.1">Collaboration Mode Determination</head><p>Given a query Q, the core objective of MasRouter is to customize an appropriate MAS from the search space S based on the complexity and domain of the query, thereby generating a sufficiently high-quality response:</p><formula xml:id="formula_4">p(a|Q) = O(a|S) F θ (S|Q) dS, S ⊂ S, (<label>4</label></formula><formula xml:id="formula_5">)</formula><p>where F θ represents the controller network parameterized by θ, which takes Q and computes the underlying distribution of S. O(•|•) denotes the conditional likelihood of obtaining the solution a by executing S. F θ is formulated as follows:</p><formula xml:id="formula_6">F θ = F θm • F θr • F θt ,<label>(5)</label></formula><p>where F θt : Q → T is the collaboration mode determiner, F θr : (Q, T ) → {R i } k i=1 denotes the role allocator, and</p><formula xml:id="formula_7">F θm : (Q, T , {R i } k i=1 ) → {M i } k</formula><p>i=1 represent the LLM backbone router. Inspired by human collaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Woolley et al., 2010;</ref><ref type="bibr">Chen et al., 2023b)</ref>, MasRouter first constructs a team management framework for the MAS using F θt , then recruits suitable talents and defines the division of tasks using F θr , and finally endows each agent with the unique intelligence through F θm . For F θt , since the relationship between collaborative modes and queries is generally difficult to characterize explicitly, we employ a variational latent model to capture their underlying semantic associations:</p><formula xml:id="formula_8">F θ t (T | Q) = pg(T | H) p h (H | Q) dH, T ∈ T (6)</formula><p>where p h (H|Q) denotes the prior probability distribution of the latent representation, and p g (T | H) decodes the probability of collaborative patterns, implemented as follows:</p><formula xml:id="formula_9">p h (H | Q) = N (H; µ t (Q), diag(σ 2 t (Q))), p g (T | H) ∝ exp( f T ψ (Q) H T τ ), τ > 0<label>(7)</label></formula><p>where µ t (•) and σ 2 t (•) obtains the mean and variance of H, respectively, and H T = g ϕ (f ψ (T ), H) embeds the relationship between the query and the collaborative patterns into the latent space. Here, f ψ : Q → R D is a text encoder (e.g., Sentence-BERT <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Reimers, 2019)</ref>, MiniLM <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wang et al., 2020)</ref>) that extracts the semantic information of the query. g ϕ : R D × R D → R D produces the refined representation of the candidate T .</p><p>With F θt , we have now customized the collaborative patterns for Q. Nevertheless, the number of agents utilized in T remains undetermined. We leverage the hidden embedding of the query to derive the number of agents k = ⌈δ(H) • γ⌉, where δ : R D → [0, 1] is a learnable complexity mapping function, and γ is the hyperparameter representing the maximum number of agents.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="4.2">Agent Role Allocation</head><p>For a MAS S = {{M i } k i=1 , {R i } k i=1 , T }, Section 4.1 has specified T and k. Subsequently, we will assign the appropriate role R i to each agent in S. Roles among different agents often have a sequential order and interdependencies. For example, we first need a programmer to write the code, and then a test engineer to validate and debug it. Correspondingly, the role allocator F θr formalizes role generation through a structured probabilistic cascade:</p><formula xml:id="formula_10">F θr ({Ri} k i=1 |Q, T ) = k ℓ=1 πr ℓ (R ℓ |Q, {Rj} ℓ-1 j=1 , T ), (<label>8</label></formula><formula xml:id="formula_11">)</formula><p>where π r ℓ denotes the probability of generating the ℓ-th role is based on Q, the selected T , and the prior ℓ -1 role profiles. We iteratively compute it as follows:</p><formula xml:id="formula_12">πr ℓ (R ℓ |Q, T , {Rj} ℓ-1 j=1 ) ∝ exp( H T R ℓ-1 HR ℓ τ ), R ℓ ∈ R, τ > 0,<label>(9)</label></formula><p>where</p><formula xml:id="formula_13">H R ℓ-1 = FFN(H∥ H T ∥ ℓ-1 j=1 H R j ℓ-1</formula><p>) denotes the implicit representation of the accumulated semantics from the role allocation process of the first ℓ -1 roles under the Q and T . H R ℓ = g ϕ (f ψ (R ℓ ), H R ℓ-1 ) captures the dynamic features exhibited by the current candidate role within the context of the previously assigned roles. Through Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_12">9</ref>), MasRouter progressively determines the roles for all agents in S. Afterward, the remaining task is to provide each agent with its driving force by routing to an appropriate LLM backbone.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="4.3">Agent LLM Routing</head><p>Each LLMs have its own strengths and drawbacks <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barandoni et al., 2024)</ref>, and the goal of LLM routing is to leverage their unique capabilities. For example, for mathematical problems, we would opt for an LLM that is particularly proficient in mathematics or one that has been specifically fine-tuned. Therefore, we posit that assigning an LLM to a specific agent primarily depends on the task's domain and difficulty, as well as their corresponding role. We implement F θm by computing the probability of selecting M i based on the query and the preceding role routing. It then views the process of LLM routing for multiple agents as a multinomial distribution problem:</p><formula xml:id="formula_14">F θm ({Mi} k i=1 | Q, T , {Ri} k i=1 ) = k n 1 ,n 2 ,...,n Nm • Nm ℓ=1 π n ℓ m (M ℓ | Q, T , {Ri} k i=1 ),<label>(10)</label></formula><p>where</p><formula xml:id="formula_15">k n 1 ,n 2 ,...,n Nm = k! n 1 !n 2 !...n Nm !</formula><p>is the multinomial coefficient. It represents the number of ways to assign k agents to N m different LLMs, with the i-th LLM selected n i times. π m denotes the probability of each LLM being selected in the global context:</p><formula xml:id="formula_16">πm(M ℓ |Q, T , {Ri} k i=1 ) ∝ exp( H T M HM ℓ τ ),<label>(11)</label></formula><p>where</p><formula xml:id="formula_17">H M = FFN(H∥ H T ∥ k j=1 H j k</formula><p>) aggregates the embedding of the query, collaborative patterns, and selected roles. H M ℓ = g ϕ (f ψ (M ℓ ), H M ) computes the latent representation of each LLM. Based on H M and H M ℓ , the compatibility between each LLM and the constructed system is obtained, which is proportional to the probability of selecting M ℓ .</p><p>As stated above, we have customized a MAS for the query. Only one final hurdle is left before achieving end-to-end training: the number of agents k becomes non-differentiable due to the rounding operation. To ensure smooth gradient flow, we replace k with its pre-rounded floatingpoint value and approximate the multinomial coefficient in Equation (10) as follows:</p><formula xml:id="formula_18">k n 1 ,n 2 ,...,n N M ≈ Γ(δ(H) • γ + 1) Γ(n1 + 1)Γ(n2 + 1)...Γ(nN M + 1) ,<label>(12)</label></formula><p>where Γ(•) denotes the Gamma function. </p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="4.4">Optimization</head><p>The optimization objective of MasRouter is presented as follows:</p><formula xml:id="formula_19">min θ E (Q,a)∼D, S∼F θ -p(a|Q) + λ • C(S; Q) (<label>13</label></formula><formula xml:id="formula_20">)</formula><p>where C(•) represents the cost evaluation of multiagent systems, and λ is the trade-off parameter. The term p(a|Q) in Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_19">13</ref>) corresponds to Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_4">4</ref>), which was computed in the previous sections. Through this optimization objective, we balance effectiveness and efficiency by maximizing the probability of generating correct solutions while minimizing token expenditure. Then following standard approaches in multi-agent structure design <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Zhuge et al., 2024;</ref><ref type="bibr">Zhang et al., 2024b)</ref>, we apply policy gradient <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Williams, 1992)</ref> to approximate and optimize Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_19">13</ref>). We summarize the notations in Appendix A, with the algorithmic workflow in Appendix B.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="5">Experiments</head></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="5.1">Experimental Setup</head></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head>Dataset and Benchmarks</head><p>We opt for MMLU <ref type="bibr">(Hendrycks et al., 2021a)</ref>, <ref type="bibr">GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021)</ref>, MATH <ref type="bibr">(Hendrycks et al., 2021b)</ref>, HumanEval <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2021)</ref>, MBPP <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Austin et al., 2021)</ref>, covering a diverse range of reasoning and problem-solving tasks. For the MATH dataset, we select 519 problems from different levels using stratified sampling.</p><p>Baselines We compare our method with (1) single-agent approaches, including COT <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Wei et al., 2022)</ref>, ComplexCoT <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fu et al., 2022)</ref>, Self-Consistency <ref type="bibr">(Wang et al., 2023b)</ref>; (2) fixed multi-agent topologies including Chain, Tree, and Complete Graph (formally defined in <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Qian et al., 2024)</ref>), LLM-Debate <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chan et al., 2023)</ref> ; (3) dynamic multi-agent systems like GPTSwarm <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Zhuge et al., 2024)</ref>, Agent-Prune <ref type="bibr">(Zhang et al., 2024b)</ref> and AFlow <ref type="bibr">(Zhang et al., 2024c)</ref>; (4) single LLM routers including PromptLLM introduced in <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Feng et al., 2024)</ref>, RouteLLM <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Ong et al., 2024)</ref>, FrugalGPT <ref type="bibr">(Chen et al., 2023a)</ref> and RouterDC <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Chen et al., 2024)</ref>. LLM Backbones We select LLMs with varying sizes and capacities, including gpt-4o-mini-0718 (OpenAI, 2024), claude-3.5-haiku <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anthropic, 2024)</ref>, gemini-1.5-flash <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Team et al., 2024)</ref> and llama-3.1-70b (Dubey et al., 2024) as the llm pool. Deepseek-v3 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024) is used to validate MasRouter's inductive capabilities. The temperature is always set as 1.</p><p>Implementation Details We set the learning rate α = 0.01, the temperature τ = 1, the cost penalty λ ∈ {5, 15, 25} and the num of iteration K ∈ {5, 10}, the agent's maximum amount γ = 6. In the MAS baselines, the number of agents equals γ. We use all the LLMs mentioned in the LLM Backbones as the candidate LLM pool for the routing method. The collaboration modes repository includes CoT, Reflection, self-consistency, LLM debate, and Macnet (Chain & Complete graph). The role pool comprises 26 roles with diverse capabilities, such as programmers using compilers and researchers with access to Wikipedia. The details of the candidate pools can be found in Appendix E.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="5.2">Performance & Cost Analysis</head><p>In this section, we compare MasRouter with twenty baselines across five benchmarks. We verify that MasRouter is: High-performing. The experimental results in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> demonstrates that MasRouter excels at constructing an effective multi-agent system. Specifically, MasRouter achieves the best performance across all of the five datasets, outperforming RouterDC, the SOTA LLM routing method, by 3.51% on average. On the MBPP dataset, MasRouter outperforms AgentPrune and AFlow by 8.20% and 1.80% at pass@1, respectively. Token-economical. <div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="5.3">Plug-in to Existing MAS</head><p>Considering that contemporary MAS is often LLMhomogeneous, i.e., relying exclusively on a single powerful model like gpt-4o, MasRouter can serve as a plug-and-play solution, seamlessly assigning an optimal LLM backbone to each agent within them, resulting in significantly less inference cost and comparable performance. In Table <ref type="table">2</ref>, we combine MasRouter with the well-established MAS methods MAD <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Du et al., 2023)</ref> and MacNet.</p><p>MasRouter improves the performance of MAD by 1.55% at pass@1 on the Humaneval dataset while reducing cost by 17.21% ∼ 28.17%. On larger datasets, the significant reduction in overhead is even more notable; when integrated with MAD, MasRouter saves the inference cost by 6.17 ∼ 7.63$ on MMLU. Overall, MasRouter can serve as a plugin to support economical multi-agent development.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="5.4">Inductive Ability Analysis</head><p>In this section, we validate that MasRouter can easily generalize to unseen LLMs without intensive re-training resources. Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> illustrates the distribution of LLMs selected by MasRouter before and after the addition of Deepseek-v3 on MMLU and MATH, with the new model being chosen 12.17% and 27.19% the time, respectively. By intelligently selecting the new, stronger model, MasRouter improved the accuracy on MMLU from 84.25% to 85.40% and also improved the accuracy on HumanEval from 90.62% to 91.41%. <div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="5.5">Framework Analysis Ablation Study</head><p>We conduct an ablation study on the four key modules in MasRouter: (1) w/o F θt , which replaces the collaboration determination F θt with random selection, (2) w/o F θr , which replaces the role allocator F θr with random selection, (3) w/o F θm , which replaces the LLM router F θr with random selection, and (4) w/o C(•), which remove the cost evaluation in Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_19">13</ref>). As shown in Table <ref type="table">3</ref>, removing the F θm results in the largest performance decline by 2.09% and 4.34%. This is because the performance of the base models on the dataset varies significantly, making selecting</p><p>The max number of agents 𝛾 Cost penalty λ the appropriate LLM to solve the problem crucial. Removing C(•) does not significantly impact the performance, but it disrupts the adaptive capability of MasRouter to query difficulty, leading to an increase in overhead by 54.09% and 41.62%.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head>Sensitivity Analysis</head><p>We analyze the sensitivity of MasRouter to two core parameters: the maximum number of the agents γ, the cost penalty coefficient λ in Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_19">13</ref>). The results are presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>. For the parameter γ, we observe a significant performance improvement as γ increases from 2 to 6 (88.50% → 90.62%).</p><p>However, further increases from 6 to 10 yield only marginal performance gains while incurring the 1.5× per-query inference costs. Considering both performance and cost, we select γ = 6. For the parameter λ, as λ increases from 5 to 25, we find that larger values lead MasRouter to favor more cost-efficient solutions, reducing the overhead by 17.78%, albeit with a slight performance degradation of approximately 1.3%. We balance effectiveness and cost by dynamically adjusting this value.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="5.6">Case Study</head><p>We present a detailed case study and visualization of the routing process of MasRouter across five benchmarks. We sincerely refer the readers to Appendix C for details.</p></div>
<div xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"><head n="6">Conclusion</head><p>In this paper, we for the first time introduce Multi-Agent System Routing (MASR), which aims to intelligently allocate collaboration patterns, agent roles, and LLMs for each query, thereby constructing a customized MAS. Based on this concept, we present MasRouter, the first highperforming, economical, and inductive MASR solution. MasRouter progressively builds a list of mutually adaptive roles, selects an LLM proficient in the task domain, and ultimately achieves a balance between effectiveness and efficiency.
